result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.all_shortest_paths()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find every shortest path between two nodes. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L45811-L45904){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.all_shortest_paths( source, target, max_paths=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![All shortest paths](/assets/graphs/all-shortest-paths.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The directed graph with three routes from A to F, unweighted. Two routes tie at two hops and both are returned: A, D, F in the accent color and A, E, F in teal. The three-hop route through B and C stays faint." width="100%"} `shortest_path()` returns one shortest route; this method returns all of them. Two paths count as distinct if they visit different nodes, so on a graph with many equally short routes (grids, lattices, dense networks) the list shows how much redundancy there is between two nodes, and which intermediate nodes every route must pass through. "Shortest" follows the same rule as `shortest_path()`: fewest hops on an unweighted graph, lowest total weight on a weighted graph (`Graph(weighted=True)`). Directed graphs are followed in edge direction. The number of shortest paths can grow exponentially with the size of the graph (a grid has a binomial number of corner-to-corner paths), so `max_paths=` can cap the result. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The starting node, as an integer ID or a string label. [target]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The destination node, as an integer ID or a string label. [max_paths]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Stop after this many paths. If `None` (default), return them all. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[list[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Each shortest path as a list of node IDs from `source=` to `target=`, sorted lexicographically by node ID. Empty if there is no path. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If a label does not exist in the graph, or a weighted graph has a negative edge weight. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} A 3 x 3 grid has six shortest paths between opposite corners, all four hops long: ::: {#ed214506 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec grid = ec.Graph().add_grid_2d(rows=3, cols=3) paths = grid.all_shortest_paths(1, 9) len(paths), paths[0] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (6, [1, 2, 3, 6, 9]) ``` ::: ::: In this diamond, B and C offer two equally short routes from A to D; the edge weights break the tie once the graph is weighted: ::: {#28f6aad3 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} edges = [("A", "B", 1.0), ("A", "C", 2.0), ("B", "D", 1.0), ("C", "D", 1.0)] hops = ec.Graph().add_nodes(list("ABCD")).add_edges(edges) weights = ec.Graph(weighted=True).add_nodes(list("ABCD")).add_edges(edges) label = hops.get_label_from_id ( [[label(n) for n in p] for p in hops.all_shortest_paths("A", "D")], [[label(n) for n in p] for p in weights.all_shortest_paths("A", "D")], ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ([['A', 'B', 'D'], ['A', 'C', 'D']], [['A', 'B', 'D']]) ``` ::: :::
